doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Gaining musicians' trust: Illinois Jacquet and Art Blakey
summary: Jacquet once asked for ten thousand dollars; Vacher says trust was rarely a problem, though stars like Blakey gave standard interviews.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Was there any problems with American black musicians with you gaining their trust?
Illinois Jacquet said he’d like ten thousand dollars if that’s what you mean. If I was to interview him.
I later interviewed him without having to pay any dollars, so I think it was all right.
Well you got farther than I did with him.
Did you? Or did I rather?
I never got past his wife I think.
Oh yes. The lady bassoon player. Carol. The current Mrs. Jacquet?
I can’t even remember. It’s been a couple of years.
Yes, that would be Carol. She forswore him from alcohol and other matters. She has been his savior he tells me.

Yeah. Fair enough. No I don’t think so. I think most of the guys that came over, I mean I’ve interviewed quite a number of older guys from New Orleans or some of the younger, sharper cats. I never sensed — because hopefully what one is conveying is enthusiasm for the music. I’m trying to say look, I’ve so much enjoyed hearing what you do, and participating in what you do, that I want to find out more and tell people something about you. And I don’t think that’s an unwelcome message for most people. Sometimes you got the sense that — I mean when I interviewed Art Blakey, because I was a feature writer for the “Melody Maker” by then, when you interviewed someone like Art Blakey, as I said to you the other night, what you got was the standard interview. “Let me tell you what I want to tell you.” And sometimes that’s difficult to break down. But it wasn’t a racial or a sort of cultural thing, it was just breaking through what was already a kind of set pattern or routine.
